name: Apollo 14’s third stage
intro: This crater was made by the third stage of the Saturn V that launched Apollo 14. After pushing the astronauts toward the Moon, the empty 14-tonne stage was steered into the ground on 4 February 1971 so seismometers could feel the crash. Look up: the see-through rocket stage over the crater shows how it looked a moment before it hit.

hotspots.title: The crater
hotspots.text: The stage blasted out a crater about 35 meters across. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it in 2009.

photo.alt: A grey, cratered moonscape seen from above, with a fresh crater and bright splashes in the middle.
photo.caption: The crater from orbit, seen by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
photo.licenseEvidence: LROC images (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University) are free for educational use with credit; this site is an educational NASA Space Apps project.

hotspots.title: One big engine
hotspots.text: This is the stage’s single J-2 engine. It burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to push the Apollo ships out of Earth orbit and onto the road to the Moon.

hotspots.title: Mostly fuel tank
hotspots.text: Nearly all of the stage is fuel tank: 17.8 meters tall and 6.6 meters across, about as tall as a six-storey building. By the time it reached the Moon its fuel was used up.

hotspots.title: Open at the top
hotspots.text: The lunar module rode to space folded up inside the top of this stage, with the command ship above it. Once the crew had pulled the lander out and flown on, the top was left open.

hotspots.title: A steep dive
hotspots.text: Unlike the lander cabins, the big stage came down steeply, about 69 degrees above the horizon, at 2.54 km per second.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Who felt it
hotspots.text: The Apollo 12 seismometer, more than 100 km away, recorded the shaking. Crashes at known times and places let scientists measure how fast vibrations travel through the Moon.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Scattered pieces
hotspots.text: Scout’s check: nothing survived in one piece. The stage broke apart on impact and its fragments are spread around the crater.

source.label: LROC (LRO camera team): the Apollo S-IVB craters

funFact: The stage weighed about 14 tonnes when it hit, more than two African elephants.
whyLeft: It was used up after sending Apollo 14 to the Moon, so NASA turned it into a giant test thump for the seismometers.
repurpose: It broke into pieces, but its scattered aluminium could one day be gathered as building material for a Moon base.

source.label: LROC: Apollo 14 S-IVB impact site, about 35 m (depth 2-3 m: Plescia et al. 2016)
